title: Enterprise Agents Have a Structure Problem - Ishita Daga, Tesla

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Ishita Daga frames enterprise agent failure as a structural problem rather than a model-capability problem. When agents give bad answers, teams reflexively seek bigger models, longer context, or more knowledge bases, but these do not address the root causes. She identifies three core problems. First, ambiguity: agents cannot determine which table, column, or knowledge base holds the cleanest or most authoritative information. Her solution is a source-of-truth hierarchy spanning three layers. The semantic layer is the cleanest, most curated source containing KPI definitions, metric calculations, and business definitions. Canonical tables offer parametric queries with moderate flexibility. The database graph connects tables, columns, and metrics for maximum flexibility but is hardest to maintain. She recommends starting with the first two layers, which solve roughly 80% of problems, before investing in the database graph. Second, staleness: context degrades as definitions, KPIs, and processes change. She proposes a context lifecycle with two components: embedding live data sources such as GitHub, CRM tools, Tableau, or DBT semantic layers that are continuously reviewed and updated, and building a feedback loop that logs correction events, evaluates agent performance through human-annotated or automated evaluation suites, and updates context accordingly. She stresses most teams underinvest in evaluation. Third, preference: different teams calculate the same metric differently, such as average milestone time measured from different reference points. Current approaches fall short—the semantic layer stores multiple calculation methods but cannot select the right one for a given user, and agent memory stores preferences but cannot distinguish between metric variants. The ideal solution would route the agent to the correct metric based on team or individual identity, but this remains an open research problem. She concludes that solving these problems requires better structure, better context management and evaluation, and ultimately embedding individual preferences to create a hive mind for data agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Enterprise agents fail due to structural problems—ambiguity, staleness, and preference—not insufficient model size or knowledge base volume.

Ambiguity is addressed through a source-of-truth hierarchy: semantic layer (cleanest, curated), canonical tables (parametric queries, flexible), and database graph (most flexible but hardest to maintain).
The semantic layer and canonical tables together solve approximately 80% of ambiguity problems; the database graph addresses the remaining 20%.
Staleness is mitigated by a context lifecycle combining live data sources (GitHub, CRM, Tableau, DBT) with a feedback loop that logs correction events and evaluates agent performance.
Most teams underinvest in evaluation, which directly contributes to agent failure and inability to track performance over time.
Preference is the hardest problem: the semantic layer stores multiple metric definitions but cannot route to the correct one, and agent memory cannot distinguish between metric variants.
The ideal preference solution routes the agent to the right metric based on team or individual identity, but this remains an open research problem.
Organizations should adopt sources of truth incrementally, starting with the easier semantic layer and canonical tables before attempting the database graph.

sections.title: Introduction and Why Agents Fail
sections.summary: Ishita Daga introduces herself as an ML engineer at Tesla building enterprise agents. She explains that when agents give bad answers, teams reflexively seek bigger models, more context, or more knowledge bases, but these do not address the root structural problems.

sections.title: Problem One: Ambiguity
sections.summary: Agents cannot determine which table, column, data source, or knowledge base to trust. Daga proposes a source-of-truth hierarchy: the semantic layer (cleanest, curated KPI definitions and metrics), canonical tables (parametric queries with flexibility), and the database graph (connects tables, columns, and metrics; most flexible but hardest to maintain). She recommends starting with the first two layers, which solve roughly 80% of problems.

sections.title: Problem Two: Staleness
sections.summary: Context degrades as definitions, KPIs, and processes change frequently. Daga proposes a context lifecycle with two components: embedding live data sources (GitHub, CRM, Tableau, DBT) that are continuously updated, and building a feedback loop that logs correction events, evaluates agent performance through human-annotated or automated evaluation, and updates context. She emphasizes most teams underinvest in evaluation.

sections.title: Problem Three: Preference
sections.summary: Different teams calculate the same metric differently, such as average milestone time measured from different reference points. The semantic layer stores multiple calculation methods but cannot route to the correct one. Agent memory stores preferences but cannot distinguish between metric variants. The ideal solution routes the agent to the right metric based on team or individual identity, but this remains an open research problem.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Daga concludes by summarizing the three problems—ambiguity, staleness, and preference—and states the need for better structure, better context management and evaluation, and ultimately embedding individual preferences to create a hive mind for data agents.

limitations: The database graph is the trickiest source-of-truth layer to build and maintain
